title: Longest Rising Chain
statement:
A sensor logs one reading per minute in `values`. A **rising chain** is a set of readings, taken in time order (they do not have to be next to each other), where every reading is **strictly larger** than the one before it.

Return the length of the longest rising chain. An empty log has length `0`.

examples.explanation: One longest chain is 2, 3, 7, 18 (another is 2, 5, 7, 101). No chain of 5 readings exists.
Equal readings do not count as rising, so a chain can only hold one reading.

hints.nudge: Look at where a chain ENDS. Of two chains with the same length, which one is easier to extend later: the one that ends on a small reading or on a large one?
hints.pattern: Keep, for each chain length, the smallest reading that a chain of that length can end with. That list stays sorted, so you can binary-search it.
hints.pseudocode:
tails = empty list (always sorted)
for each x in values:
  p = first position in tails with tails[p] >= x
  if p is past the end: append x
  else: tails[p] = x
return size of tails
hints.walkthrough: A simple answer: best[i] = 1 + the largest best[j] over earlier readings j with values[j] < values[i]; the answer is the largest best[i]. That is O(n^2). To go faster, let tails[k] be the smallest possible last reading of a rising chain with k + 1 readings. tails is always sorted, so for each new reading x binary-search the first tail that is >= x (equal values must REPLACE, not extend, because the chain is strictly rising). Replace that tail with x, or append x when it is larger than every tail. The size of tails is the answer. Note that tails itself is not a real chain, only its length is meaningful. O(n log n). Python: bisect_left. C++: lower_bound.
